pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Block Periodization: Breakthrough in Sport Training (Issurin, 2008) — ingest map

PDF is real text: 221 pages, `extract_pdf.py --probe`: `{"pages": 221, "text_pages": 221,
"scanned": false}`. Publisher: Ultimate Athlete Concepts, 2008.

**Print-to-PDF page offset = +11**: the 0-based PDF index = printed page + 11 (a PDF viewer,
and the Read tool's `pages` parameter, show printed + 12 instead; do not cite viewer/Read
page numbers as if they were the 0-based index). Verified at five
independent chapter starts, not just the offset's origin point: Ch1 (printed 1 = PDF 12,
"Block periodization vs. traditional theory"), Ch2 (printed 36 = PDF 47, "The Workout:
general concepts and structure guidelines"), Ch3 (printed 76 = PDF 87, "Microcycles,
mesocycles and training stages"), Ch4 (printed 125 = PDF 136, "Long-term preparation"),
Ch5 (printed 160 = PDF 171, "Altitude training"). Glossary starts printed 202 = PDF 213.
The offset holds unchanged front matter through at least PDF 213 of 221; no evidence of a
mid-book repagination.

**Note on the extractor's `--pages A-B` flag (updated during Batch 2):** as of this session
the extractor was fixed and `--pages A-B` is now **inclusive** (returns pages A through B).
Each page also now carries `viewer_page` (index + 1) alongside `page` (still the 0-based
index used for all citations in this book's entries: keep citing `page`, not `viewer_page`).
Earlier note, kept for history: during Chapter 1's first pass, when the flag was still
end-exclusive, two pages (PDF 25 and 44) were missed and recovered with a follow-up call
before atomizing. That failure mode no longer applies with the inclusive flag, but an extra
requested page beyond the end still does no harm.

**Confidence rule for this book:** `proven` is reserved for physiology/mechanics established
independent of this text (e.g. CNS fatigue and motor-unit recruitment order, connective
tissue/warm-up basics already `proven` elsewhere in this library). Issurin's own periodization
theory, block-sequencing prescriptions, and the numeric tables he or his co-authors derived
(residual-effect durations, key-exercise interval tables, the ≤3-modality/65-70% workout rule)
are capped at `supported`: they are a single author's synthesis of Soviet/Israeli
sport-science practice and secondary citations, not independently replicated in this ingest.
Single-case coaching anecdotes (Bondarchuk's podium sweep, the author's own 1985 canoe-kayak
program) are `untested`. `contested` is set where this text conflicts with a claim already
in this library, named explicitly both ways. Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation"
(Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`), is full-text cached in this
library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`
(ingested 2026-07-31, not "not yet cached" as an earlier version of this note said). The
principle entry cites it for a direct contradiction of the 2008 low/mid-level carve-out (its
p.11). Its concentrated-unidirectional critique (pp.6-7) targets Verkhoshansky's model, not
this book's A-T-R model; the training-stage entry treats it as a caveat on the 28-study
support figure for that reason, not a contradiction.

| # | Chapter | Printed pp | PDF idx | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|-----------|---------|--------|---------|
| 1 | Block Periodization vs. traditional theory | 1-35 | 12-46 | done | 8 |
| 2 | The Workout: general concepts and structure guidelines | 36-75 | 47-86 | done | 8 |
| 3 | Microcycles, mesocycles and training stages | 76-124 | 87-135 | done | 12 |
| 4 | Long-term preparation | 125-159 | 136-170 | pending | 0 |
| 5 | Altitude training | 160-201 | 171-212 | pending | 0 |
| — | Glossary / About the author | 202-end | 213-221 | skip | n/a (reference matter, not atomized) |

**Chapter 1 section map** (for locator precision, corrected during the Ch1-2 review pass):
1.1 Traditional theory (printed 1-20, PDF 12-31); 1.2 The Block Periodization Concept
(printed 20-30, PDF 31-41, contains the accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy and
Table 1.6 residual-effect durations); 1.3 Consequences of the modern approach (printed
30-33, PDF 41-44, starts at printed 30 / PDF idx 41, not printed 31 as an earlier version of
this map said); Summary (printed 32-33, PDF 43-44); References (printed 34-35, PDF 45-46,
not atomized).

**Chapter 2 section map** (corrected during the Ch1-2 review pass): 2.1 Workout
classifications (printed 36-45, PDF 47-56); 2.2 Workout structure (warm-up, main part,
cool-down) (printed 46-59, PDF 57-70); 2.3 Guidelines for constructing a workout — sequencing,
compatibility, daily series (printed 59-69, PDF 70-80, starts at printed 59 / PDF idx 70,
not printed 60); 2.4 How to structure a workout / Summary (printed 69-72, PDF 80-83);
References (printed 73-75, PDF 84-86, not atomized; the reference list runs through printed
75 / idx 86, not printed 73 / idx 84 as an earlier version of this map said, though no
substantive content is missing from the atomized entries).

**Chapter 3 section map**: 3.1 Microcycles (printed 76-101, PDF 87-112): 3.1.1-3.1.2 types and
load-wave design (printed 77-80, PDF 88-91); 3.1.3 aerobic/strength-aerobic microcycle, Popov
example (printed 81-85, PDF 92-96); 3.1.4 anaerobic glycolytic microcycle (printed 86-89, PDF
97-100); 3.1.5 explosive-strength microcycle, Sedykh example (printed 90-93, PDF 101-104);
3.1.6 pre-competitive (tuning) microcycle (printed 93-96, PDF 104-107); 3.1.7 in-season
team-sport microcycle, names American football (printed 97-100, PDF 108-111); 3.1.8 how to
construct a microcycle (printed 100-102, PDF 111-113). 3.2 Mesocycles (printed 102-116, PDF
113-127): 3.2.1 accumulation (printed 102-106, PDF 113-117); 3.2.2 transmutation (printed
106-111, PDF 117-122); 3.2.3 realization/taper (printed 111-116, PDF 122-127). 3.3 Training
stage (printed 116-121, PDF 127-132): 3.3.1 competition within the stage, Popov example
(printed 117-118, PDF 128-129); 3.3.2 prolonging residual training effects, mini-blocks
(printed 118-120, PDF 129-131). Summary (printed 120-121, PDF 131-132); References (printed
122-124, PDF 133-135, not atomized).

_Batch 1: built the chapter map and atomized Chapters 1-2, per the ingest review gate's
two-stage process — stopping cleanly at the Chapter 2/3 boundary so the Codex falsification
review (`staging/review_block-periodization-issurin_codex.md`) can run on a complete,
self-contained unit before Chapter 3 begins._

_Batch 2 (this session): atomized Chapter 3 in full (PDF 87-135, printed 76-124, 12 entries:
8 framework, 3 case-study, 1 heuristic, 0 claim; see entry list in the session report). Gave
the most careful treatment to 3.1.6 (pre-competitive microcycle), 3.2 (accumulation/
transmutation/realization mesocycles in full prescriptive detail), and 3.3.2 (prolonging
residual training effects via mini-block insertion) per the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap. The first pass claimed every
cited table and figure matched the page image; the round-1 review (2026-09-27,
`staging/review_issurin_ch3_opus.md`) found four misreads: Figure 3.7 (AM/PM content
inverted), Table 3.7 (Impact/Restoration durations swapped), Figure 3.10 (a fall "to" about
69% conflated with the text's "by up to 69.3%") and Figure 3.11 ("erased" where both markers
stay above baseline). All four were corrected against the page images in the fix pass
(`staging/fixes_issurin_ch3_applied.md`), which also re-checked Figures 3.8 and 3.12 (this
book is real text, not scanned, per the probe above). Extractor note: mid-session the extractor's `--pages A-B`
behavior changed from end-exclusive to inclusive; this batch's extraction (run before the
change, requesting 87-136 to get pages 87-135) and all page citations (the extractor's 0-based
`page` field) are unaffected._

_Batch 3 (recommended next): Chapter 4, Long-term preparation (PDF 136-170, printed 125-159) —
annual and quadrennial cycles, long-term athlete development, sensitive periods, talent
identification. Directly relevant to Baylor's multi-year athlete development question._

_Batch 4 (lowest priority for football): Chapter 5, Altitude training (PDF 171-212, printed
160-201). Recommend framework-only treatment (5-15 entries, confidence capped at `untested`)
or skipping entirely unless Eric names a specific altitude-camp use case — Baylor football
does not train at altitude as a standard practice per anything in `method-baseline.md`._

# Review: Issurin, *Block Periodization* (2008), Chapter 3 (Opus falsification pass, round 1)

Reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5, 2026-09-27. Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md` plus `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`.
Scope: the 12 entries in `staging/_scope_issurin_ch3.txt` (folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/block-periodization--issurin/`). The Ch1-2 entries were read for duplicates and contradictions only, not graded.
Source: `Block Periodization - Issurin.pdf`. Chapter 3 (idx 87-135, printed 76-124) was extracted in full with PyMuPDF and read. Every table and figure cited by an in-scope entry was rendered and read as a page image: Tables 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.12, 3.13; Figures 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.8, 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 (3.12 zoomed).
Primary-source spot checks: I pulled the Europe PMC abstracts for three studies the chapter retells: Hooper et al. 1995, Cardinale & Stone 2006 and Margaritis et al. 2003.

## Locator convention

- Entries cite the **0-based PDF index = printed + 11**. That holds on every Ch3 page. A viewer shows printed + 12. Below, "idx N / p.M" means index N, printed page M.
- Only one entry locator is wrong: the Cardinale & Stone case is on **idx 104 / p.93**, not idx 103 / p.92. All other page locators check out.

## Global findings (apply across rows; not repeated per row)

- **G1 Unlabelled writer voice (recurring from Ch1).** Every **Example** in scope is an invented football or Baylor scenario, or a generic walk-through, with no "Inference:" prefix. The "Population caveat:" paragraphs are unlabelled too, and so are the "this is the entry most directly answering the miss-log gap" openers. Most of these are reasonable; they just need the label. The "Inference, mapped to a college football calendar" headers are correctly labelled, which is an improvement on Ch1.
- **G2 Em dashes: clean.** The only em dashes are the house-style bold section headers. The Ch1 body-prose problem did not recur.
- **G3 False "verified against page image" stamps.** Four entries (and `_book.md`) claim page-image verification for content that the page image contradicts:
  - Figure 3.7: the entry inverts the AM/PM content.
  - Table 3.7: the "3-6 days" comment belongs to the Impact row, not Restoration.
  - Figure 3.10: the figure shows expenditure falling **to** about 69%. The text says "by up to 69.3%".
  - Figure 3.11: the entry's title says the gains were "erased", but both markers stay above baseline.

  `_book.md` says all Ch3 tables and figures "matched exactly". That is false; correct it when these rows are fixed.
- **G4 The Issurin 2016 vault brief is still unlinked.** No Ch3 entry links `research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`. Its line 57 ("does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football") and line 58 (the multi-targeted conclusion "should not be treated as settled comparative evidence") belong in When NOT for the accumulation, transmutation, realization and prolonging entries.
- **G5 Supercompensation as the taper mechanism.** The pre-competitive and realization entries both rest "Why it works" on supercompensation (idx 106 / p.95; idx 122 / p.111). That is the author's stated mechanism, so plain text is correct. Both entries should add `[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]` (staging, `contested`) to Related.
- **Confidence:** no `proven` rating is used anywhere in scope. The three case studies are correctly `untested`. The framework entries are at the `supported` ceiling. The one `contested` entry (transmutation) is mis-grounded; see its row.

## Entry table

Severity tags: **[major]** means the source is misstated in substance; **[minor]** means a locator, wording, omission or labelling problem.

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md` | FIX | [minor] (1) When NOT reads "the specific number-of-peaks guidance ... is stated for individual-sport training loads". The book restricts one-peak designs to "sufficiently prepared high-performance athletes but not ... novice and less prepared athletes" (idx 90 / p.79). It proposes the 5-point scale precisely for "non-measurable sports like sailing or team and dual sports" (idx 89 / p.78), and Fig 3.2's last session can be "a match in team or dual sports" (idx 91 / p.80). (2) When to apply calls "a normal in-season game week" Issurin's **competitive** microcycle. Table 3.1 defines that type as "participation in competition", with high to very high load (idx 88 / p.77). The book treats the in-season team week as a separate design (3.1.7, idx 108 / p.97). (3) Why it works credits the peak-trough logic to the concentration principle (writer synthesis). The author's own reason is on idx 90 / p.79: "The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes' restoration and stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high demand workouts." (4) The entry omits that the impact microcycle needs a special restoration program (diet, supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, relaxation) (idx 89 / p.78). (5) The "impact week concept sometimes used informally" is an uncited general claim. (6) Example unlabelled (G1). Verified: all Table 3.1 cells (idx 88 / p.77); adjustment shortened to 3-5 days and restoration 3-4 days mid-season (idx 88 / p.77); "used most widely" (idx 89-90 / pp.78-79); one-peak quotes (idx 90 / p.79); Fig 3.2 structure, ten workouts, Issurin 2003 (idx 91 / p.80); three benefits of the point scale (idx 91-92 / pp.80-81). | (1) Replace with: "Inference: the peak-count guidance is stated by athlete preparedness, not sport type (idx 90 / p.79); the book proposes the point scale for team and dual sports (idx 89 / p.78), but gives no team-sport outcome data." (2) Rewrite: "Inference: an in-season game week is closest to the 3.1.7 maintenance design, not Table 3.1's competitive type (participation in competition, high to very high load, idx 88 / p.77)." (3) Cite the author's reason with its locator, and label the concentration link "Inference:". (4) Add the impact restoration requirement with its locator. (5) Delete or cite the "impact week" clause. (6) Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |
| `case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle.md` | FIX | [major] **The author's mechanism for the headline claim is missing.** The title and point (c) say glycolytic work is nearly absent. The book's reason is on idx 93-94 / pp.82-83: "The athlete's body can not respond effectively to training stimuli that simultaneously affect very different physiological systems. Highly intense glycolitic workloads cause a profound metabolic response and hormonal shift that can last two-three days (Viru, 1995) ... The addition of anaerobic glycolitic workloads, however, leads to a disruption in metabolic adaptation and dramatically decreases the cumulative training effect." The entry's Why it works gives only the aerobic plus strength oxidation rationale. It also omits the book's counterweight: the combination "reduces strength increases in comparison to strength training alone (Zatsiorsky, 1985)" (idx 92 / p.81). [minor] (1) "Addressing the problem raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case" is unlabelled synthesis, and backwards: Ch1's case is aerobic work suppressing strength, while the p.81 problem is enlarged muscle lacking oxidative capacity. (2) "Popov's coach" and "rather than only in the weight room" are not in the text (the book says "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski, personal communication", idx 93 / p.82). (3) The 24-hour rule is stated for "developing workouts for maximal strength" after "exhaustive aerobic training" (idx 95 / p.84). Figure 3.4 (idx 96 / p.85) still places medium or substantial MS sessions on the afternoons after morning AE (Mon, Thu), and puts the key MS workout (Wed AM) 24 h after the Tue AM AE key-workout, with only a low-load session between. The entry states the rule without that scope. (4) Why it works says the 24 h "follows directly from the testosterone/cortisol citation". That citation gives "many hours"; 24 h is the author's rule, supported by Chesley's ≥24 h protein turnover after resistance work. (5) Example unlabelled (G1). Verified: ten workouts, AT and Tech dominant, MS daily in medium proportions, AP in 3 workouts, SE large, AnG once in the 200 m stepwise test (idx 93 / p.82); takeaways a-c (idx 93 / p.82); compatible modalities, maximum strength first priority (idx 94 / p.83); all Table 3.2 cells (idx 95 / p.84); Viru, Karelson & Smirnova 1992 and Chesley 1992 (idx 95 / p.84); Komi fast-motor-unit point (idx 95 / p.84). | Add to Why it works, as plain author text: "Issurin's reason for excluding glycolytic work: training stimuli that hit very different systems at once conflict; glycolytic loads cause a metabolic and hormonal shift lasting 2-3 days (Viru 1995) that disrupts the aerobic adaptations (capillarization, aerobic enzymes, myoglobin, mitochondria) built during recovery (idx 93-94 / pp.82-83)." Add: "The combination also reduces strength gains vs strength training alone (Zatsiorsky 1985, idx 92 / p.81)." Label the Ch1 link "Inference:" and fix its direction. Write "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski (personal communication)". Scope the rule: "applies to development max-strength workouts after exhaustive aerobic work; Figure 3.4 still places medium or substantial MS sessions the afternoon after morning AE (Mon, Thu; idx 96 / p.85)." Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |
| `framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design.md` | FIX | [minor] (1) When NOT reads "this section's evidence ... is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports". The author lists four benefits: coaches can validate the test set, individual norms can be established, athletes learn their own responses, and self-regulation and body-mass methods can be set in advance. 3. **The one-week microcycle has no physiological rationale** (idx 87 / p.76). It rests on "social life" (school, work, weekends). Training camps allow shorter or longer cycles. This is a direct source for the baseline's "a training week need not equal 7 calendar days" (method-baseline line 145), and would replace the microcycle-types entry's loose baseline tie-in.
4. **Impact microcycles need a special restoration program** (idx 89 / p.78): diet, supplements, hydrotherapy, massage and mental relaxation "in order to fulfill their goals". Relevant to any "hardest camp week" mapping.
5. **Specialised strength exercises should duplicate the competition technique** (Yessis 2006, idx 103 / p.92). The coach must understand the skill and build the strength exercise to simulate it, so technique and strength improve together. Check the vault's dynamic-correspondence entries before writing, since this may be only a link.

## Source quirks to record (not entry errors)

- "(see 3.3.3)" at idx 119 / p.108: there is no 3.3.3; the material is 3.3.2.
- "taking into account the optimal timing for different training modalities (Figure 3.3)" at idx 99 / p.88: Figure 3.3 is Popov's chart. Figure 2.3 is the timing figure.
- Komi is cited as 1989 in the text (idx 95 / p.84) and 1988 in the references (idx 134 / p.123). Viru & Viru is 2000 in the text (idx 104 / p.93) and 2001 in the references (idx 135 / p.124).
- The kayaker improvement rate: 5.9% over 3 weeks is 1.97%/wk, but the book prints 1.93 (idx 114 / p.103).
- Energy expenditure "by up to 69.3%" in the text vs about 69% of baseline in Figure 3.10 (idx 126-127 / pp.115-116).
- Three case studies are retold with sample sizes or conclusions that differ from their primary abstracts: Hooper (19 vs 14), Margaritis (20 vs 7 + 9), and Cardinale & Stone (pooled-sex r not flagged).

## Notes for `_book.md` (out of scope; not graded)

- Its claim that all Ch3 tables and figures "matched exactly" against the page images is false (G3: Figure 3.7, Table 3.7, Figure 3.10, Figure 3.11).
- Its Issurin 2016 "not yet cached" sentence is still wrong (Ch1 G4).
- The Ch3 section map and the entry counts (8 framework, 3 case-study, 1 heuristic) are correct.

## Reciprocal-link suggestions

- Transmutation entry → vault `research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-...md` and `mccall-2023-...subjective...md`.
- Pre-competitive and realization entries → staging `supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md`.
- Accumulation, transmutation, realization and prolonging entries → vault `research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`.
- Prolonging entry ↔ Ch1 `framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle.md` (already one-way; its "special measures" line should link back).

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** 0 GO, 12 FIX, 0 NO-GO.

- Every number in Tables 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.8-3.14 and in the kayaker, Snell, Hooper (as the book tells it), Cardinale and triathlete passages matches the page.
- No `proven` rating is used. The case studies are correctly `untested`.
- Body-prose em dashes are gone.
- The taper and peaking entries are rated `supported`, which is the right ceiling. Neither duplicates a vault entry; the vault has no taper entry.

The failures are figure readings stamped "verified", source mechanisms merged or supplied, and the Ch1 labelling pattern (G1, G4) recurring.

Fixes, in priority order:

1. **Pre-competitive:** rewrite the Figure 3.7 description. The morning sport-specific key-workouts are the point of the design.
2. **Popov competition:** fix the title ("erased" is false: V-AT 1.57 → 1.63 → 1.60) and separate the hormonal and glycolytic (Volkov) chains.
3. **Prolonging mini-blocks:** fix the Example (no mini-block needed at 4-5 weeks; the 6-week arithmetic fails). Replace the invented mechanism with the author's "Apparently" hedge and state that no outcome data is given. Describe all Figure 3.12 patches. Add the "rigid and inflexible" caveat.
4. **Accumulation:** fix the Table 3.7 Options assignment, add the "three weeks or less" band, and fix the title.
5. **Transmutation:** re-ground or drop `contested` (recommend `supported`, with the baseline moved to When NOT). Add the Hooper primary-abstract discrepancy (n = 14, circular staleness definition, catecholamines added prediction). Credit the 5 bpm signal to its sources.
6. **Realization:** record the Figure 3.10 vs "69.3%" inconsistency and the Margaritis abstract discrepancy. Add the taper-mood sentence, the Fitz-Clarke tension and the G5 link.
7. **Sedykh:** fix the locator (idx 104 / p.93), add the pooled-sex confound, and fix the title scope.
8. **Popov aerobic:** add the author's glycolytic-exclusion mechanism, the Zatsiorsky strength trade-off, and the scope of the 24-h rule against Figure 3.4.
9. **In-season:** fix the Example against Figure 3.8 (Tue and Wed AM key lifts, Thu PM key practice, Fri off, Sunday game; shift one day for Saturday). Change "mesocycles" to "microcycles".
10. **Minor rows** (microcycle types, anaerobic glycolytic, construction heuristic): the labels and wording given in each row.
11. **Globals:** G1 labels on every Example and Population paragraph, G4 Issurin 2016 links, G5 supercompensation link, and correct `_book.md`'s "matched exactly" claim.

# Round-2 review: Issurin, *Block Periodization*, Chapters 1-2 (fix verification)

Reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5, 2026-09-27. Read-only pass over the 16 Ch1-2 entries and the Ch1-2 parts of `_book.md` after the fixes logged in `staging/fixes_issurin_ch1-2_applied.md`. Ch3 files (`_scope_issurin_ch3.txt`) were not reviewed.

Method: I read every in-scope file in full and extracted the PDF text for idx 12-86 (PyMuPDF). I rendered Figure 2.3 (idx 71) as an image and checked its bar ends. Every quote or locator the fixer added or changed was checked against the page. I opened the vault briefs for every new citation (Issurin 2016, Comyns 2013, McLaren 2017, Hanson 2007, Hirayama 2014, Seitz 2017), the Bompa and Verkhoshansky entries they link to, and `week1-lecture.md`. Issurin 2016 was also read in the original (Zotero `PT9QTQ2I`, PDF pp. 6, 7, 11). Locators below use the book's convention: 0-based idx = printed + 11.

All cited vault and staging files exist: the three PAP papers, Comyns, McLaren, Issurin 2016, Bompa `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching` / `framework--step-loading-paradigm` / `heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio`, the Moyer Bondarchuk file, and the four Verkhoshansky staging entries. The problems are in what three of them are cited *for* (rows below).

## Read this first: round 1 was wrong about Issurin 2016 (do not re-apply its correction)

Round 1 told the fixer to re-ground `contested` in the principle and training-stage entries on the vault brief for Issurin (2016). The brief says concentrated-unidirectional evidence was "insufficient" for combat, team-sport and swimming preparation [its p.6] and "restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" [its p.11]. The fixer applied this exactly. **The correction was itself wrong.** The original paper shows:

- The "concentrated unidirectional (CU)" model is **Verkhoshansky's**, not Issurin's. Table 1 is "based on Verkhoshansky [9, 10]". The p.6 findings (basketball, handball and soccer fitness gains with no game data; swimmers 2 of 3) all come from Table 2, "Effects of concentrated unidirectional bloc periodization training programs".
- Issurin's own A-T-R model is the **multi-targeted BP** version. Section 3 starts at p.7, and p.11 names the canoe-kayak, track and swimming lineage. The review reports it is "supported by the findings of 28 studies" [p.11].
- The review does not soften the 2008 critique of the traditional model; it repeats it. CU "has no advantage over traditional planning, because it does not allow the multi-peak annual design" [p.6]. The conclusion also reads: "It would be a regrettable mistake to think that the traditional theory of training should stay the same" [p.11].

So the 2016 review cannot "dispute" the 2008 line "does not work well for high-performance athletes". Both entries now misstate a library source.

**There is a real Issurin-vs-Issurin contradiction to use instead.** It sits on the principle entry's own When NOT carve-out:

- 2008 (PDF 44 / p.33): the traditional approach "has visible benefits for the preparation of low- and mid-level athletes ... medium-level concentration still provides sufficient stimulation".
- 2016 [p.11]: "proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration". It also cites a recreational-trainee study where the block program was "considerably superior".

**Upstream note (the fixer cannot act on it; flag to Eric):** the vault brief `research-papers/issurin-2016-...md` never says that "concentrated-unidirectional" means Verkhoshansky's model, which is why this misreading happened. Its Key findings should be annotated: "CU = Verkhoshansky's model; the multi-targeted (A-T-R) model is the one the review favours."

|---|---|---|---|---|
| `principle--concentration-of-training-workloads.md` | FIX | **NEW PROBLEM** [major] | (1) The Contested paragraph says the 2008 "does not work well for high-performance athletes" claim (PDF 19 / p.8, verified) "is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review", which "judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient". That finding is about Verkhoshansky's CU model (Issurin 2016 pp.6-7, Table 1 "based on Verkhoshansky"). The same review supports multi-targeted BP with 28 studies and restates the critique of the traditional model (p.6, p.11); see the section above. (2) The Eric's-baseline sentence is garbled: "...not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle", incompatible qualities are not both trained...". Checked and fixed: link to `[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]` works; Table 1.4 "There is sufficient energy supply" locator note matches idx 20; Fig 1.7 quotes (idx 37); low/mid carve-out (idx 44); Bompa 1984 (idx 13); Bompa inference relabelled; week1-lecture.md lines 1795 and 1838 confirm the Issurin attribution and "Can't ride 2 horses". | Replace the whole Contested paragraph with: "**Contested (Issurin 2008 vs Issurin 2016):** this book limits the concentration principle to high-level athletes, saying medium-level concentration 'still provides sufficient stimulation' for low- and mid-level athletes (PDF 44 / p.33). Issurin's later review says 'proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration' (Issurin 2016, p.11, `research-papers/issurin-2016-...`). The same review restricts only Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, where many interacting abilities are needed (pp.6-7). It supports Issurin's own multi-targeted block model (28 studies, p.11) and repeats the 2008 critique of traditional planning, so it does not dispute 'does not work well for high-performance athletes' (PDF 19 / p.8). Its 28-study support is an author-curated, non-systematic synthesis." Keep `contested`, with this as the stated reason. Rewrite the baseline sentence: "Eric's baseline: the course teaches this rule from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67), filed as 'you can't ride two horses with one saddle': incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, ... class1 transcript pp.28-29)." """Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))

14	# The Long-Term Sequential Development Model
15	
16	**What it is** — A pyramid model for an athlete's career: a broad base of **multilateral development** (childhood) → increasing **specialized training** (junior years) → **high performance** (maturity). The proportion of sport-specific work rises as the athlete matures — very small during the multilateral phase, then growing; for advanced athletes, ~60–80% of training time is sport-specific, the rest developing biomotor abilities (the exact ratio varies by sport: ~90% specific in long-distance running, ~40% in high jump). Bompa gives per-sport guideline ages for *starting training*, *starting specialization*, and *reaching peak performance* (e.g. specialization generally not before ~14–15 in most sports; Russian longitudinal data suggested not before age 15).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Three longitudinal studies (East German 14-year, Russian survey, and a tennis study) found athletes with a strong multilateral base reached higher ultimate performance, with fewer overuse injuries and less burnout, than early specializers — who progressed faster initially but plateaued, lost confidence, and faced more pressure. The base builds the physiological and psychological capacity that specialization later draws on.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Designing youth/developmental pathways; resisting pressure to specialize a fast-developing young athlete too early; setting sport-appropriate specialization timing; setting the general→specific ratio by training age.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Some early-entry sports (women's gymnastics, figure skating, diving, swimming) legitimately require young specialization due to early peak ages — the model bends to the sport's maturation demands. The guideline ages are rough, not prescriptive per individual (use [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Deepens [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]].
23	
24	**Example** — A talented 12-year-old showing rapid sport-specific progress is deliberately kept on a broad multilateral program, with specialization phased in around 14–15, to protect the long-term performance ceiling rather than chase early wins.
25

13	
14	# Biological vs Chronological vs Training Age
15	
16	**What it is** — Three different "ages" govern how much and what kind of training an athlete can tolerate, and they often disagree: **Chronological age** (years lived), **Biological age** (maturational status — best indexed by sexual maturation / circulating testosterone), and **Training age** (years of structured preparation). Prescribe to the limiting one, not to chronological age by default.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Biological age predicts physical performance potential better than chronological age — more biologically mature athletes are stronger, faster, and better at team sports than same-aged peers. Training age determines readiness for specialization: a high chronological age with a *low* training age still needs multilateral and skill work, not an advanced specialized load. Youth generally tolerate higher *volume* at *moderate* load better than high-intensity/high-load work; combining heavy load with high volume raises musculoskeletal injury risk in the young.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Grouping and prescribing for youth/developing athletes; spotting the late-maturer being out-competed by early-maturers of the same chronological age; deciding whether an athlete is ready to specialize.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat the early-maturer's current dominance as durable talent — biological-age advantages wash out as peers mature. And don't read training age off the calendar; an older athlete new to structured training has a low training age. Pairs with [[principle--individualization]] and [[framework--ltad-sequential-model]].
23	
24	**Example** — Two 14-year-olds: the early-maturer handles a heavier base, while the late-maturer with the same chronological age is kept on multilateral, moderate-load work rather than being pushed to match — protecting development and reducing injury risk.
25

Training age determines readiness for specialization: a high chronological age with a *low* training age still needs multilateral and skill work, not an advanced specialized load. **When NOT to apply** — Don't treat the early-maturer's current dominance as durable talent — biological-age advantages wash out as peers mature. And don't read training age off the calendar; an older athlete new to structured training has a low training age. Pairs with [[principle--individualization]] and [[framework--ltad-sequential-model]].

13	
14	# Multilateral Development Before Specialization
15	
16	**What it is** — Broad, general physical development — endurance, strength, speed, flexibility, coordination — provides the training foundation for success in all sports and should precede sport-specific specialization. Athletes who build a strong multilateral base tolerate later sport-specific work better and reach a higher ultimate ceiling.
17	
18	**Why it works** — A wide base of biomotor abilities raises work capacity and resilience, so the athlete can absorb more specific training later without breaking down. For young athletes especially, multilateral development reduces injury potential; combined with fatigue management (injury risk rises sharply when fatigue is high), it protects long-term progression.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Early-career and youth program design; off-season base-building; setting the general preparation phase before sharpening toward competition.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The base is a *foundation*, not a permanent diet. Mature, high-level athletes need progressively more sport-specific work; staying too general too long under-prepares them for competition demands (counterweight: [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]]). The right balance shifts with training age — more multilateral when young, more specific when advanced. The career-long sequence and the empirical evidence for it are detailed in [[framework--ltad-sequential-model]]; readiness to specialize is judged by [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]], not the calendar.
23	
24	**Example** — A freshman collegiate athlete spends the first training blocks developing general strength, coordination, and work capacity across varied modalities before the program narrows toward position-specific power and speed qualities in later years.
25	
26	**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]]: the Russian sport-school age table is a concrete data source for the same multilateral-before-specialization claim

# Multilateral Development Before Specialization

**What it is** — Broad, general physical development — endurance, strength, speed, flexibility, coordination — provides the training foundation for success in all sports and should precede sport-specific specialization. Athletes who build a strong multilateral base tolerate later sport-specific work better and reach a higher ultimate ceiling.

**Why it works** — A wide base of biomotor abilities raises work capacity and resilience, so the athlete can absorb more specific training later without breaking down. For young athletes especially, multilateral development reduces injury potential; combined with fatigue management (injury risk rises sharply when fatigue is high), it protects long-term progression.

**When to apply** — Early-career and youth program design; off-season base-building; setting the general preparation phase before sharpening toward competition.

**When NOT to apply** — The base is a *foundation*, not a permanent diet. Mature, high-level athletes need progressively more sport-specific work; staying too general too long under-prepares them for competition demands (counterweight: [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]]). The right balance shifts with training age — more multilateral when young, more specific when advanced. The career-long sequence and the empirical evidence for it are detailed in [[framework--ltad-sequential-model]]; readiness to specialize is judged by [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]], not the calendar.

**Example** — A freshman collegiate athlete spends the first training blocks developing general strength, coordination, and work capacity across varied modalities before the program narrows toward position-specific power and speed qualities in later years.

**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]]: the Russian sport-school age table is a concrete data source for the same multilateral-before-specialization claim

14	# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)
15	
16	**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
17	begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
18	system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
19	gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
20	13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
21	sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
22	strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
23	era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24	24-25.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
27	existing long-term athletic development material: early specialization in
28	strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
29	and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
30	specialization later draws on. The text does not itself restate this mechanism in this
31	passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
32	evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25). The text does note one exception: "many Russian
33	experts" hold that early specialization is possible in sports emphasizing coordination,
34	agility, flexibility, or speed (e.g. gymnastics), because of the pre-adolescent's
35	particular ability in those respects; strength and endurance sports are discouraged for
36	youngsters specifically (printed 25).
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a more granular, sport-by-sport reference
39	table alongside this library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric
40	detail beyond, the Bompa library's
41	[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
42	Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
43	break it out by individual sport; this convergence is this entry's own comparison, not
44	stated in either source.
45	
46	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table,
47	not a modern, population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies
48	(see [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
49	Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football, not listed in Table 1.2 at
50	all) do not map cleanly onto these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as
51	illustrative, not prescriptive, for a Baylor Athletics context; this caution is this
52	entry's own judgment.
53	
54	**Example** — **Inference:** The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
55	supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
56	early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
57	in this library.

61	that concretize this framework's general specialization-age guidance),

1	---
2	type: library-entry
3	kind: framework
4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
5	book: block-periodization--issurin
6	chapter: "3.2.1"
7	topic: accumulation mesocycle duration, content, monitoring
8	category: [periodization, mesocycle, accumulation, programming]
9	confidence: supported
10	ingest-tier: full-text
11	created: 2026-09-26
12	---
13	
14	# Accumulation Mesocycle: Up to Six Weeks for Deep Change, Three Weeks or Less to Refresh, 10-14 Days Late-Season
15	
16	**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
17	introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
18	(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
19	printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
20	basic abilities, aerobic endurance and maximal strength, both requiring "profound morphological
21	and even organic changes," versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
22	supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
23	program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
24	endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
25	114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
26	sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (the book prints this as a 1.93%/week
27	improvement rate; arithmetically 5.9% over 3 weeks is 1.97%/week, recorded here as a source
28	quirk, not corrected); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14
29	weeks added only 0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness
30	program was "very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six
31	weeks, and had only a minor effect for the next 14 weeks," directly supporting BPC's case for
32	shorter, higher-turnover blocks over long, continuous ones. The general adaptive-decline
33	concept itself is cited to Bouchard (1986); the further claim that aerobic-endurance programs
34	show "similar trends" is given uncited in the text (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104). Based on this,
35	Issurin sets the following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks**
36	when training is intended to elicit "more profound physiological changes" (typically early
37	season, when athletes are less calendar-constrained); **three weeks or less** when training is
38	intended "to stimulate basic abilities and refresh general responses"; **10-14 days** at
39	season's end, when important competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by
40	sequencing microcycle types (Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105; re-verified against the
41	page image, 2026-09-27): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle (if starting a new
42	training stage, not needed after a transition period) followed by an adjustment microcycle
43	(can be shorter than a week); the **mid-and-end** part is built from loading microcycles, whose
44	count sets the mesocycle's total length; **options**, an impact microcycle (about 3-6 days)
45	"can be administered in the mid-part," and a restoration microcycle "can be planned immediately
46	after impact McC and followed by a loading McC" (the 3-6 day duration belongs to the impact
47	option, not the restoration option). General load-shape rule: increase load gradually at the
48	start, hold maximal load in the middle, and reduce load at the end so the next mesocycle
49	(transmutation) begins without excess fatigue; in special cases, a 3-4 day restorative
50	microcycle can be inserted near the end of accumulation for this purpose.
51	Monitoring (Table 3.8, PDF p. 117, printed p. 106; verified against page image) tracks three
52	categories: **workload performance** (total weekly mileage, total sport-specific reps/week,
53	key-workout outcomes, each compared actual-vs-planned, week-to-week, and across the season);
54	**targeted (basic) abilities** (time-trial results, free-weight-trial results, average
55	key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
56	heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
57	trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
58	training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
59	weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.
60	
61	**Why it works** — The kayaker case study is offered as direct evidence for the general
62	biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
63	time" (Bouchard, 1986): diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed
64	training emphasis, which is the physiological argument for keeping each mesocycle-block short
65	and switching emphasis rather than running one long undifferentiated program.
66	
67	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Fall camp** functions
68	as a short accumulation mesocycle at the low end of Issurin's range (closer to the 10-14 day
69	figure, or the 3-4 week figure if camp's aerobic/strength-base emphasis is counted from
70	voluntary summer conditioning): given the diminishing-returns pattern in the kayaker case
71	(most of a strength/aerobic gain arrives in the first 3-6 weeks), a multi-month, undifferentiated
72	summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against; a shorter,
73	concentrated base-building window, followed by a shift to more specific work, is the BPC
74	alternative. **The gap between the last regular-season/conference-championship game and a bowl
75	game** (commonly roughly 3-5 weeks for many programs) is long enough to support a short
76	accumulation mesocycle (10-14 days to three weeks, matching this section's end-of-season and
77	"three weeks or less, refresh" bands) if the goal is to rebuild any basic-ability
78	deterioration accumulated over a long season before shifting into a bowl-specific
79	transmutation/realization sequence. Note that Figure 3.12's 20-25-day figure (used later in
80	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]) is that section's own accumulation
81	**and** transmutation duration for a 7-9 week training stage, not a mini-block length; it
82	should not be conflated with the bowl-gap estimate here.
83	
84	**When NOT to apply** — The kayaker case study is a single unpublished thesis
85	(Sharobajko, 1984, a Ph.D. dissertation, Moscow All-Union Research Sport Institute), n = 8,
86	female kayakers, with no control group not receiving the same 20-week program; it demonstrates
87	a within-group improvement-rate curve, not a controlled comparison against an alternative
88	mesocycle length. Issurin's own qualifier on the kayaker case: it applies "among qualified
89	athletes having high levels of general fitness," where "relatively short periods of
90	accentuated workloads provide substantial improvement" (PDF p. 113, printed p. 102).
91	**Inference:** the kayakers were "highly qualified," so this duration-band evidence may not
92	hold for lower-training-age players; that qualifier belongs alongside the population caveat
93	below, not just the general-fitness framing. **Inference, population caveat:** this is
94	Issurin's own book-wide pattern: the accumulation-duration guidance and its supporting evidence
95	are drawn from individual/endurance Olympic sports (kayaking) tracking isometric strength and
96	presumably aerobic markers, not from any team-contact-sport population; football's basic-ability
97	profile (short-duration high-force efforts, position-specific demands, large roster with
98	heterogeneous training age) is not represented in this evidence base at all. The specific
99	duration bands (six weeks / three weeks or less / 10-14 days) are Issurin's own applied
100	judgment, not derived from a stated formula connecting them to the kayaker data's exact decay
101	curve. Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states that evidence for block periodization
102	"spans dissimilar sports and training levels" and "does not supply validated block durations or
103	effect estimates for collegiate American football" (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, vault
104	`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
105	
106	**Example** — **Inference:** a 3-4 week early-summer strength-aerobic emphasis block,
107	monitored against Table 3.8's indicators (weekly key-lift totals, a repeated time-trial or
108	aerobic test, resting HR trend, body composition), gives a coach a citable structure for when
109	to expect most of a block's gain to already have happened. The kayaker curve itself shows most
110	of a **20-week** program's gain arriving in the first 3-6 weeks; it says nothing about how gain
111	is distributed inside a much shorter 3-4-week block, so treat "most of the gain arrives early"
112	as a directional caution transplanted from a longer program, not a claim about where inside a
113	short block the gain concentrates.
114

# Accumulation Mesocycle: Up to Six Weeks for Deep Change, Three Weeks or Less to Refresh, 10-14 Days Late-Season

**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
basic abilities, aerobic endurance and maximal strength, both requiring "profound morphological
and even organic changes," versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (the book prints this as a 1.93%/week
improvement rate; arithmetically 5.9% over 3 weeks is 1.97%/week, recorded here as a source
quirk, not corrected); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14
weeks added only 0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness
program was "very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six
weeks, and had only a minor effect for the next 14 weeks," directly supporting BPC's case for
shorter, higher-turnover blocks over long, continuous ones. The general adaptive-decline
concept itself is cited to Bouchard (1986); the further claim that aerobic-endurance programs
show "similar trends" is given uncited in the text (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104). Based on this,
Issurin sets the following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks**
when training is intended to elicit "more profound physiological changes" (typically early
season, when athletes are less calendar-constrained); **three weeks or less** when training is
intended "to stimulate basic abilities and refresh general responses"; **10-14 days** at
season's end, when important competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by
sequencing microcycle types (Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105; re-verified against the
page image, 2026-09-27): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle (if starting a new
training stage, not needed after a transition period) followed by an adjustment microcycle
(can be shorter than a week); the **mid-and-end** part is built from loading microcycles, whose
count sets the mesocycle's total length; **options**, an impact microcycle (about 3-6 days)
"can be administered in the mid-part," and a restoration microcycle "can be planned immediately
after impact McC and followed by a loading McC" (the 3-6 day duration belongs to the impact
option, not the restoration option). General load-shape rule: increase load gradually at the
start, hold maximal load in the middle, and reduce load at the end so the next mesocycle
(transmutation) begins without excess fatigue; in special cases, a 3-4 day restorative
microcycle can be inserted near the end of accumulation for this purpose.
Monitoring (Table 3.8, PDF p. 117, printed p. 106; verified against page image) tracks three
categories: **workload performance** (total weekly mileage, total sport-specific reps/week,
key-workout outcomes, each compared actual-vs-planned, week-to-week, and across the season);
**targeted (basic) abilities** (time-trial results, free-weight-trial results, average
key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.

**Why it works** — The kayaker case study is offered as direct evidence for the general
biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
time" (Bouchard, 1986): diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed
training emphasis, which is the physiological argument for keeping each mesocycle-block short
and switching emphasis rather than running one long undifferentiated program.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Fall camp** functions
as a short accumulation mesocycle at the low end of Issurin's range (closer to the 10-14 day
figure, or the 3-4 week figure if camp's aerobic/strength-base emphasis is counted from
voluntary summer conditioning): given the diminishing-returns pattern in the kayaker case
(most of a strength/aerobic gain arrives in the first 3-6 weeks), a multi-month, undifferentiated
summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against; a shorter,
concentrated base-building window, followed by a shift to more specific work, is the BPC
alternative. **The gap between the last regular-season/conference-championship game and a bowl
game** (commonly roughly 3-5 weeks for many programs) is long enough to support a short
accumulation mesocycle (10-14 days to three weeks, matching this section's end-of-season and
"three weeks or less, refresh" bands) if the goal is to rebuild any basic-ability
deterioration accumulated over a long season before shifting into a bowl-specific
transmutation/realization sequence. Note that Figure 3.12's 20-25-day figure (used later in
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]) is that section's own accumulation
**and** transmutation duration for a 7-9 week training stage, not a mini-block length; it
should not be conflated with the bowl-gap estimate here.

**When NOT to apply** — The kayaker case study is a single unpublished thesis
(Sharobajko, 1984, a Ph.D. dissertation, Moscow All-Union Research Sport Institute), n = 8,
female kayakers, with no control group not receiving the same 20-week program; it demonstrates
a within-group improvement-rate curve, not a controlled comparison against an alternative
mesocycle length. Issurin's own qualifier on the kayaker case: it applies "among qualified
athletes having high levels of general fitness," where "relatively short periods of
accentuated workloads provide substantial improvement" (PDF p. 113, printed p. 102).
**Inference:** the kayakers were "highly qualified," so this duration-band evidence may not
hold for lower-training-age players; that qualifier belongs alongside the population caveat
below, not just the general-fitness framing. **Inference, population caveat:** this is
Issurin's own book-wide pattern: the accumulation-duration guidance and its supporting evidence
are drawn from individual/endurance Olympic sports (kayaking) tracking isometric strength and
presumably aerobic markers, not from any team-contact-sport population; football's basic-ability
profile (short-duration high-force efforts, position-specific demands, large roster with
heterogeneous training age) is not represented in this evidence base at all. The specific
duration bands (six weeks / three weeks or less / 10-14 days) are Issurin's own applied
judgment, not derived from a stated formula connecting them to the kayaker data's exact decay
curve. Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states that evidence for block periodization
"spans dissimilar sports and training levels" and "does not supply validated block durations or
effect estimates for collegiate American football" (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, vault
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).

**Example** — **Inference:** a 3-4 week early-summer strength-aerobic emphasis block,
monitored against Table 3.8's indicators (weekly key-lift totals, a repeated time-trial or
aerobic test, resting HR trend, body composition), gives a coach a citable structure for when
to expect most of a block's gain to already have happened. The kayaker curve itself shows most
of a **20-week** program's gain arriving in the first 3-6 weeks; it says nothing about how gain
is distributed inside a much shorter 3-4-week block, so treat "most of the gain arrives early"
as a directional caution transplanted from a longer program, not a claim about where inside a
short block the gain concentrates.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],

[[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]].
